# Figures for publication

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Figures for publication";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the arctic fox has the most insulating fur measured in any mammal. Its lower critical temperature is below [−40 °C]{.hl}: above that, it keeps warm without raising its metabolic rate.

_Source: Prestrud (1991), Arctic_
:::

## Where we are

You already know how to build a plot in `ggplot2`, and the details are one search away. This lecture is about the decisions that no function makes for you: what to show, how to show it honestly, and how to get it onto the page of a thesis or a journal.

. . .

A figure is part of the evidence. Readers should be able to judge it for themselves, including those who print in greyscale or see colours differently.

## Today

1. Show the data
2. Less is more
3. Models and uncertainty
4. Publication-ready

## The data {.smaller}

The lexical decision data from lecture 1: 30 participants (15 L1, 15 L2 speakers of English), 40 words each.

```{r}
set.seed(2027)
participants <- tibble(participant = sprintf("P%02d", 1:30),
                       group = rep(c("L1", "L2"), each = 15),
                       p0 = rnorm(30, 0, 60),
                       p1 = rnorm(30, 0, 12))
words <- tibble(word = sprintf("w%02d", 1:40),
                log_freq = runif(40, 1, 6),
                length = pmin(pmax(round(11 - 1.1 * log_freq + rnorm(40, 0, 1.6)), 3), 13),
                w0 = rnorm(40, 0, 30))
lex <- crossing(participants, words) |>
  mutate(slope = -25 + p1 + if_else(group == "L2", -25, 0),
         rt = round(700 + p0 + w0 + if_else(group == "L2", 120, 0) +
                    slope * (log_freq - 3.5) + 12 * (length - 7) + rnorm(n(), 0, 70))) |>
  select(participant, group, word, log_freq, length, rt)
```

# Show the data

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` an arctic fox's winter fur is nearly [twice as long]{.hl} as its summer fur.

_Source: Underwood & Reynolds (1980), report for the Office of Naval Research_
:::

## What a reader needs

To judge a difference between groups, a reader needs the [size]{.hl} of the difference, the [variability]{.hl} in the data and the [sample size]{.hl}.

. . .

A bar chart of group means shows only the size of the difference.

## The dynamite plot {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
lex |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rt), se = sd(rt) / sqrt(n()), .by = group) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = pandan, width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.15, colour = mist)
```

A [dynamite plot]{.hl} shows two numbers for 1,200 responses from 30 people. The bars suggest values from zero up to the mean, and the SE treats all 600 responses per group as independent.

## What bars hide

```{r bars-hide, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
set.seed(3)
hidden <- bind_rows(
  tibble(group = "Construction A", y = rnorm(60, 4, 0.9)),
  tibble(group = "Construction B", y = c(rnorm(30, 2.6, 0.35), rnorm(30, 5.4, 0.35))),
  tibble(group = "Construction C", y = c(3.1, 3.7, 4.3, 4.9))
) |>
  mutate(y = y - mean(y) + 4, .by = group)
p_bar <- hidden |>
  summarise(y = mean(y), .by = group) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, y)) +
  geom_col(fill = kingfisher, width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(title = "The bars", x = NULL, y = "Mean rating")
p_pts <- ggplot(hidden, aes(group, y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(title = "The data", x = NULL, y = NULL)
p_bar + p_pts
```

Three sentence types with the same mean acceptability: one bell shape, two clusters of speakers, and only four ratings.

## Which points? {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
p_trials <- ggplot(lex, aes(group, rt)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.1, colour = kingfisher) + labs(title = "Trials")
p_people <- lex |>
  summarise(rt = mean(rt), .by = c(participant, group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, rt)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) + labs(title = "Participants")
p_trials + p_people
```

Plot the [unit of analysis]{.hl} your claim is about. A difference between groups of speakers is a claim about participants: show participant means.

## Show the data {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
participant_means <- summarise(lex, rt = mean(rt), .by = c(participant, group))
ggplot(participant_means, aes(x = group, y = rt)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, colour = muted, size = 2.5) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, fun.args = list(mult = 1.96),
               colour = kingfisher, size = 0.9, linewidth = 1.3,
               position = position_nudge(x = 0.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean RT per participant (ms)")
```

Every participant, plus the group mean and its 95% confidence interval, moved to the side so it hides no points.

## Which error bar?

```{r errorbars, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.0}
l1 <- filter(participant_means, group == "L1")$rt
tibble(type = factor(c("± 1 SD", "± 1 SE", "95% CI"), levels = c("± 1 SD", "± 1 SE", "95% CI")),
       half = c(sd(l1), sd(l1) / sqrt(length(l1)), qt(0.975, length(l1) - 1) * sd(l1) / sqrt(length(l1)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = type, y = mean(l1))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean(l1) - half, ymax = mean(l1) + half),
                  colour = kingfisher, size = 0.9, linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean RT, L1 participants (ms)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16, colour = mist))
```

- The [SD]{.hl} describes the spread of the data; the [SE]{.hl} and the [CI]{.hl} describe the precision of the mean
- The same 15 participants give three very different bars: always say in the caption which one you show

## Distributions: raincloud {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(lex, aes(x = rt, y = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_density_ridges(jittered_points = TRUE, position = "raincloud", colour = mist,
                      alpha = 0.6, scale = 0.7, point_colour = mist, point_alpha = 0.2, point_size = 0.7,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
  labs(x = "RT (ms)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

A [raincloud plot]{.hl} from `{ggridges}` shows the shape of the distribution above, the observations below, and a line at the median.

## Axes

- A bar shows a value by its [length]{.hl}, so its axis must start at zero
- Points and lines show values by [position]{.hl}, so their axis can zoom in on the range that matters

Free scales in facets and log scales are fine as long as the axis title or caption says so.

## Say what you did

In the caption or axis titles, tell the reader:

- What the error bars or ribbons are: SD, SE or a confidence interval, and for which unit
- Whether points are raw data, participant means or model predictions
- How many observations each group has
- Whether an axis is on a log scale or does not start at zero
- Whether points are jittered or lines smoothed
- Whether any data were excluded, how many, and why

# Less is more

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` arctic foxes come in two genetically fixed colour phases. The [white]{.hl} phase is white only in winter; the [blue]{.hl} phase is dark all year.

_Sources: Prestrud (1991), Arctic; Norwegian Polar Institute_
:::

## Before and after

```{r before-after, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
pm <- participant_means
p_before <- ggplot(pm, aes(group, rt, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(L1 = "red", L2 = "green")) +
  labs(title = "Before", x = "group", y = "rt") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 16, base_family = plot_font) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "grey85"))
p_after <- ggplot(pm, aes(group, rt)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA, colour = muted, fill = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, colour = kingfisher, size = 2) +
  labs(title = "After", x = NULL, y = "Mean RT per participant (ms)") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
p_before + p_after
```

## What changed

- The legend repeated the `x` axis, so it went
- Red and green separated nothing the axis did not already separate, and fail for many readers
- Axis titles became words with units; `x` needs no title when the labels say it all
- The grey background, heavy grid and outlines added ink but no information
- We kept the points, because they show the data

## Colour for every reader

- Choose a [qualitative]{.hl}, [sequential]{.hl} or [diverging]{.hl} palette from the type of variable: categories, low to high, or distance from a meaningful midpoint
- Red–green colour-vision deficiencies are common, especially among men, and figures are printed in greyscale and shown on dim projectors
- The [Okabe–Ito]{.hl} palette keeps eight colours distinct for the common deficiencies, and is built into `R` 4.0 or later

```{r}
okabe <- unname(palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito"))
group_colours <- c(L1 = okabe[2], L2 = okabe[3])
```

## Redundant coding {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
word_group_means <- summarise(lex, rt = mean(rt), .by = c(word, log_freq, group))
ggplot(word_group_means, aes(x = log_freq, y = rt, fill = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = floor_col, stroke = 0.6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(L1 = 21, L2 = 24)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colours) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Mean RT per word (ms)", fill = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Colour and shape show the same variable ([redundant coding]{.hl}), so the groups survive greyscale. The named vector keeps each group's colour across all figures.

## Order categories {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
word_means <- summarise(lex, rt = mean(rt), .by = c(word, log_freq))
twelve <- filter(word_means, word %in% sprintf("w%02d", 1:12))
p_alpha <- ggplot(twelve, aes(x = rt, y = word)) + geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3)
p_ordered <- ggplot(twelve, aes(x = rt, y = fct_reorder(word, rt))) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3) + labs(y = "word")
p_alpha + p_ordered & labs(x = "Mean RT (ms)")
```

Alphabetical order is rarely the order that matters. `fct_reorder()` sorts the categories by a value, here the mean RT.

## Spaghetti

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
ggplot(lex, aes(x = log_freq, y = rt, group = participant, colour = group)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Fitted RT (ms)", colour = NULL)
```

In this [spaghetti plot]{.hl}, thirty overlapping lines make it impossible to follow any one participant.

## Small multiples with context {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
some <- filter(lex, participant %in% c("P01", "P02", "P16", "P17"))
others <- rename(lex, id = participant)
ggplot(some, aes(x = log_freq, y = rt)) +
  geom_smooth(data = others, aes(group = id), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              colour = vine, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = group), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ participant, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Fitted RT (ms)", colour = NULL)
```

In these [small multiples]{.hl}, the grey layer has no `participant` column, so it appears in every panel.

## Things to avoid

- Pie charts ask readers to compare angles and areas, which they do badly; bars or points work better
- With two different `y` axes on one plot, the choice of scaling decides what looks related
- 3D effects, shadows and textures add ink without information
- Rainbow palettes for continuous values
- Bars that do not start at zero, and bars for means without the data

# Models and uncertainty

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` arctic foxes prepare for winter food shortages by storing [fat]{.hl} and caching food during summer and autumn.

_Source: Prestrud (1991), Arctic_
:::

## Raw data or model?

- Raw data show what was observed, including what the model leaves out
- A model shows the estimated effects, adjusted for the other predictors, with their uncertainty
- A good figure often shows both: the model as lines and ribbons, the data behind it

## The ribbon of `geom_smooth()` {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
ggplot(lex, aes(x = log_freq, y = rt, colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "RT (ms)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

This ribbon comes from a separate `lm()` for each group that treats all 600 responses as independent. It ignores the [repeated measures]{.hl}, so it is too narrow.

## The model

```{r}
lex <- lex |>
  mutate(freq_c = log_freq - mean(log_freq),
         length_c = length - mean(length),
         group = factor(group))
contrasts(lex$group) <- contr.sum(2)
m4 <- lmer(rt ~ freq_c * group + length_c + (1 + freq_c | participant) + (1 | word),
           data = lex)
```

The same model as in lecture 1, now to be shown in a figure.

## Predictions with `{ggeffects}` {.smaller}

```{r}
pred <- ggpredict(m4, terms = c("freq_c", "group")) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(log_freq = x + mean(lex$log_freq))
pred
```

Predicted RTs for each group across the frequency range, with `length_c` held at its mean (0), and 95% confidence intervals from the fixed effects.

## Your own prediction plot {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
ggplot(pred, aes(x = log_freq, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_point(data = word_group_means, aes(y = rt), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "RT (ms)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Lines and ribbons: mixed-model predictions with 95% CIs. Points: word means.") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

`ggpredict()` returns a data frame, so the plot is an ordinary `ggplot()` that you can style like any other.

## A coefficient plot {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.5}
coef(summary(m4)) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(low = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`, high = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Estimate, y = fct_rev(fct_inorder(term)))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), colour = kingfisher, size = 0.8, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (ms) with 95% Wald interval", y = NULL)
```

A [coefficient plot]{.hl} has one row per fixed effect. It works best when there are many predictors on the same scale.

## Which plot for a model?

[Predictions]{.hl} show effects in the units of the outcome, which makes them the better choice for interactions and non-linear effects. [Coefficients]{.hl} are compact, but each estimate depends on coding and centering, so readers also need the model specification.

. . .

In both cases, say which predictors are held constant, and at which values.

# Publication-ready

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` among arctic mammals up to the size of an [arctic fox]{.hl}, bigger species have longer winter fur. Larger species, such as wolves and caribou, all have about the same fur length.

_Source: Scholander et al. (1950), as summarised by Underwood & Reynolds (1980)_
:::

## Titles that say something

```{r, eval = FALSE}
labs(title = "Frequency speeds up L2 speakers more than L1 speakers",
     subtitle = "Mixed-model predictions with 95% confidence intervals",
     caption = "30 participants, 40 words. Points: word means.")
```

- On slides and posters, a title that states the finding tells the audience what to look for
- In papers, the journal's caption usually takes that role: put the finding in the first sentence of the caption

## Reference lines and notes {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(participant_means, aes(x = group, y = rt)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(participant_means$rt), colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.45, y = mean(participant_means$rt), label = "grand mean",
           colour = muted, vjust = -0.5, size = 5) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean RT per participant (ms)")
```

`annotate()` adds one element at fixed coordinates, without a data frame.

## Labels that move aside {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.9}
slowest <- slice_max(word_means, rt, n = 5)
ggplot(word_means, aes(x = log_freq, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = slowest, aes(label = word), colour = mist, size = 5,
                  min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.6, seed = 1) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Mean RT per word (ms)")
```

`{ggrepel}` places labels so they do not overlap each other or the points. Label only the points the text talks about.

## Combining figures {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.4}
p_pred <- ggplot(pred, aes(x = log_freq, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Predicted RT (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
p_raw <- ggplot(participant_means, aes(x = group, y = rt, colour = group)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, size = 2.5) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean RT (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
(p_raw | p_pred) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & labs(colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

`{patchwork}`: `|` side by side, `/` on top, `&` for every panel. `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` merges identical legends.

## A theme for the paper {.smaller}

```{r}
theme_paper <- function(base_size = 11, base_family = "") {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90"),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
          plot.title.position = "plot",
          legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

Write the [theme function]{.hl} once, keep it in a file, and `source()` it at the top of every script for the same paper. `theme_set(theme_paper())` makes it the default.

## The theme in use {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.9}
p_pred +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_colours) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colours) +
  labs(colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_paper(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Panel B again, with the paper's theme and the Okabe–Ito colours.

## Size on the page

```{r sizes, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.0}
tibble(size = c("8 cm wide", "17 cm wide", "30 cm wide"), width = c(8, 17, 30)) |>
  mutate(text_pt = 11 * width / 17, size = fct_inorder(size)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = size, y = text_pt)) +
  geom_col(fill = kingfisher, width = 0.55) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(text_pt, 1), " pt")), vjust = -0.5, colour = mist, size = 5.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 23)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Text size on the page") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16, colour = mist))
```

A figure made 17 cm wide with 11 pt text, then shrunk or stretched to fit: the text shrinks or grows with it. Make the figure at its final size.

## Exporting with `ggsave()`

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fig1 <- (p_raw | p_pred) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
ggsave("figures/figure1.pdf", fig1, width = 17, height = 8, units = "cm")
ggsave("figures/figure1.png", fig1, width = 17, height = 8, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
```

- Set width and height to the size on the page: often about 8.5 cm for one column and 17 cm for the full width; check the journal's guidelines
- Use the same `base_size` in your theme for every figure, so all text matches the body text

## Vector or raster?

| | Vector (`.pdf`, `.svg`) | Raster (`.png`, `.tiff`) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Made of | shapes and text | pixels |
| Zoom | sharp at any size | blurry when enlarged |
| Best for | most plots | plots with very many points; some journals |
| Size setting | width and height | width, height and `dpi` (300 for print) |

. . .

Never paste a screenshot of the RStudio plot pane into a thesis or a paper.

## Before you submit

- Does each figure answer one clear question?
- Can the reader see the data, the variability and the sample size?
- Do the caption and axes say what the points, error bars and ribbons are?
- Are axes labelled in words, with units?
- Does it work in greyscale and for colour-blind readers?
- Is the text readable at the final size?
- Is the code saved, so you can redraw the figure when a reviewer asks?

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Show the [data]{.hl}, at the level of the unit your claim is about, with variability and sample size
- Say what error bars and ribbons are; SD, SE and CI answer different questions
- Remove what carries no information; order categories by something meaningful; use small multiples instead of spaghetti
- Choose palettes that work for colour-blind readers and in greyscale, and code key groups twice
- Plot [model predictions]{.hl} with their uncertainty over the raw data; `geom_smooth()` ignores repeated measures
- Make figures at their [final size]{.hl}, in a vector format, with one [theme function]{.hl} for the whole paper
:::

- Lüdecke, D. (2018). ggeffects: Tidy data frames of marginal effects from regression models. _Journal of Open Source Software_, 3(26), 772.
